::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Squeeze Theorem problem with two variables](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4640570/squeeze-theorem-problem-with-two-variables), asked by [NDD](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1072114/ndd) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-02-16; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I am asked to find $$\lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}\left(\sin(3x-y)\cos\left(\frac{1}{x^2+y^2}\right)\right)$$
> I know the answer is 0, but I have to prove it. 
> I know that $\cos{\frac{1}{x^2 + y^2}}$ is bound between -1 and 1, but I am not quite sure how to set up the full squeeze theorem.
:::

> I know that $\cos{\frac{1}{x^2 + y^2}}$ is bound between -1 and 1

This means that
$$\left| \sin(3x-y) \cos{\frac{1}{x^2 + y^2}} \right| \leq \left|\sin(3x-y)\right|$$
Furthermore $|\sin(t)| \leq |t|$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$. So $|\sin(3x-y)| \leq |3x-y|$.

Does that help?
